summary: Argues that IPv6 does not need NAT to get the benefits people often attribute to it, such as some management and security properties. It describes how to get local network protection in IPv6 using other mechanisms, such as firewalls and address planning. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 networks can use firewalls and address-management techniques to protect local devices without changing packet addresses. This RFC explains the available approaches and the gaps that still needed work when it was written.

questions: how to protect a local network with ipv6
how do ipv6 privacy addresses work
how to hide network topology in ipv6
how can ipv6 protect a local network
subtitle: IPv6 network protection methods that do not depend on address translation

tldr.problem: Network address translation is often used in IPv4 networks for more than address conservation, including filtering and topology hiding. IPv6 has a different address model, so those goals need not depend on translation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes local network protection using firewall policy, privacy addresses, unique local addresses, prefix delegation and methods for hiding topology.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational guidance describing approaches and trade-offs, not a best-current-practice document or a configuration manual.

today: RFC 4864 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document describes IPv6 Local Network Protection approaches and identifies areas for further standards work.

sections.title: NAT Functions and IPv6 Local Protection
sections.content:
Network address translation (NAT) changes addresses in packets. The RFC notes that IPv4 operators also rely on effects associated with NAT, such as stateful filtering, hiding internal addresses and independent control of local addressing. These functions are not the same as address translation itself.

IPv6 Local Network Protection (LNP) uses a defined boundary between the local network and outside networks while preserving address transparency where needed. The document is Informational: it describes possible ways to meet management and security goals, but does not prescribe one approach or provide a network configuration manual.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT changes packet addresses, but operators may want other things from the same device, such as filtering or hiding internal structure. This RFC describes ways to meet those goals in IPv6 without relying on address translation.

sections.title: IPv6 Addressing Tools
sections.content:
Privacy addresses change the interface identifier over time to make it harder to link separate activities to one device. Unique Local Addresses (ULAs) provide locally scoped addresses that do not need to be advertised on the public Internet. A network can use ULAs for local communication and global addresses for communication outside the site.

DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation lets a router request a prefix for local use. The RFC also describes untraceable addresses, which separate the address visible outside a site from the device's physical place in the internal topology. That approach needs internal routing support, such as host routes or a tunnel through a Home Agent.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 offers several address choices for different purposes. Temporary addresses can reduce tracking, local addresses can support communication inside a site, and delegated prefixes can provide addresses for external communication.

sections.title: Firewalls, Privacy and Topology Hiding
sections.content:
A stateful firewall can allow return traffic for connections started from inside while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic. The RFC recommends firewall and intrusion-detection protection where a site wants a boundary, and notes that correct configuration remains necessary. IPv6 address size can make remote subnet scanning more difficult, but this is not a substitute for security controls.

Privacy addresses can make it harder to track an individual host, while randomized subnet assignments or indirection can make internal topology harder to infer. The stronger topology-hiding approaches can add internal routing complexity, route-table scale concerns or tunnel overhead. ULAs have no intrinsic security properties; their useful feature here is their limited routing scope by default.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall can block incoming connections that were not requested from inside the network. Address choices can also make it harder to track a device or infer where it sits, but each method has operational costs.

sections.title: Applying the Tools to Different Networks
sections.content:
The case studies describe medium and large private networks, small private networks, single-user connections and service-provider networks. A larger site might use ULAs for stable internal communication and a delegated global prefix for external access. A small network may receive a prefix through DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation.

The RFC emphasizes combining tools according to the local goal. A firewall provides filtering; privacy addresses limit some forms of device profiling; untraceable addresses or tunnels can hide topology. Its conclusion is that these mechanisms can provide the perceived benefits of NAT while avoiding address translation, but the approaches have different requirements and trade-offs.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks can combine these tools in different ways. A large site may prioritize stable internal addresses and topology hiding, while a small site may use a delegated prefix and a stateful firewall.

sections.title: Gaps and Conclusion
sections.content:
The RFC identifies areas where additional standards or best-practice documentation would help, including dynamic firewall pinhole management, combining privacy addresses with topology masking, and site multihoming. It says these gaps do not prevent LNP from being used in many scenarios, but they affect how completely the approaches can meet all goals.

The document concludes that IPv6 LNP can provide firewalling, topology hiding and privacy without changing packet addresses. It does not claim that any single mechanism supplies all of these functions or removes the need for sound network security.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says IPv6 networks can protect local systems without translating addresses. It also identifies work that would make some protection and management approaches easier to apply.
